title: Distributed Cache
subtitle: Multi-node distributed in-memory caching: Consistent Hashing, W-TinyLFU eviction, and cache stampede defense.
keyTakeaways: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes limits key remapping to ~1/N of the keyspace when cache nodes join or leave, preventing cache-miss avalanches against backend databases.
Inside individual cache nodes, pairing concurrent hash lookups with segmented eviction lists (or W-TinyLFU) achieves O(1) performance without global lock contention across CPU cores.
Defend against the three classic cache failure modes: Cache Stampede (Singleflight coalescing), Cache Penetration (Bloom filters / negative caching), and Hot Keys (L1 near-cache).

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A Distributed Cache stores high-frequency data in memory across a cluster of nodes, reducing backend database load and delivering sub-millisecond read latencies.
bullets: Functional: Support `GET(key)`, `SET(key, value, ttl)`, and `DEL(key)` operations across a cluster of storage nodes.
Functional: Configurable eviction policies (LRU, LFU, FIFO) to reclaim memory when cache nodes reach capacity.
Non-Functional: Sub-millisecond read latency (p99 < 1ms on local network) with high horizontal read scalability.
Non-Functional: High availability with automatic shard rebalancing when cache nodes fail or scale up.
Out of Scope: Persistent ACID transactional ledgers, cross-datacenter multi-region consensus, and complex secondary index queries.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: A large-scale caching tier handles heavy read throughput with strict latency constraints.
bullets: Throughput: 1,000,000 read QPS and 50,000 write QPS across the cluster.
Data Size: 100 million active items with an average object size of 5 KB = ~500 GB of raw cached data.
Cluster Sizing: Sizing with 2x memory headroom for fragmentation and eviction buffers yields ~1 TB of cluster RAM, distributed across 16 nodes with 64 GB RAM each.
Network Throughput: 1,000,000 reads/sec * 5 KB = 5 GB/s of egress bandwidth across the cluster (~312 MB/s per node, requiring 10 Gbps network interfaces).

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Calculating memory and network requirements shows that distributed caches are typically network-bound or CPU-bound rather than memory-constrained.
bullets: Memory sizing: 100M items * (5 KB payload + 64 bytes metadata) = ~506 GB. Budgeting 1 TB allows for hot-key redundancy and overhead.
Node count calculation: 16 cache nodes provide 1 TB of total RAM and aggregate network bandwidth of 160 Gbps, comfortably absorbing 40 Gbps of read traffic.
Eviction rate: At 50,000 writes/sec with full memory, the cluster evicts ~50,000 old keys/sec, making low-overhead eviction algorithms essential.

codeSnippet.title: Distributed Cache Capacity Estimation Worksheet
codeSnippet.code:
================================================================================
                  DISTRIBUTED CACHE CAPACITY ESTIMATION SHEET
================================================================================
1. THROUGHPUT & QPS (150B Cache Operations / Day, 10:1 Read:Write Ratio)
   - Average Read QPS           : 136B / 86,400      = ~1,574,000 QPS
   - Peak Read QPS (3x)         : 1.574M * 3         = ~4,722,000 QPS
   - Average Write QPS          : 14B / 86,400       = ~162,000 QPS
   - Peak Write QPS (3x)        : 162K * 3           = ~486,000 QPS
   - Total Peak Cluster QPS     : 4.72M + 0.49M      = ~5.21 Million QPS

2. CLUSTER MEMORY (RAM) & SHARD SIZING
   - Active Keys in Working Set : 3,000,000,000 (3 Billion keys)
   - Average Entry Footprint    : 64B key + 2048B val + 64B LRU/dict = ~2.13 KB
   - Raw Primary RAM            : 3B * 2.13 KB       = ~6.39 TB
   - Primary RAM (+25% Headroom): 6.39 TB * 1.25     = ~8.0 TB
   - Total RAM with HA Replicas : 8.0 TB * 2 (RF=2)  = 16.0 TB
   - Node Topology (64GB nodes) : 160 Primary Shards + 160 Replica Shards
   - Peak QPS per Primary Shard : 5.21M / 160        = ~32,560 QPS / node

3. 5-YEAR SNAPSHOT / WARM-RESTART STORAGE (EBS / S3 RDB Checkpoints)
   - Rolling RDB Checkpoint Size: 6.4 TB compressed (~3.2 TB per snapshot)
   - 7-Day Rolling Snapshots    : 3.2 TB * 7         = ~22.4 TB (Constant over 5 yrs)

4. NETWORK BANDWIDTH
   - Peak Ingress (Writes)      : 486K QPS * 2 KB    = ~972 MB/sec (7.8 Gbps total)
   - Peak Egress (Reads)        : 4.72M QPS * 2 KB   = ~9.44 GB/sec (75.5 Gbps total)
   - Per-Shard Network Load     : 9.44 GB/s / 160    = ~59 MB/sec (472 Mbps / shard)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Use lightweight binary protocols (like Redis RESP or Memcached binary protocol) over persistent TCP/gRPC connections to minimize serialization overhead.
bullets: Wire protocol: Binary commands for `GET`, `SET`, `MGET`, and `DELETE` with explicit 32-bit TTL values and integer payload lengths.
Internal node storage: Keys and values stored in contiguous off-heap memory buffers or slab allocators to minimize garbage collection pauses.
Metadata headers: 16 bytes per entry storing TTL expiration timestamp, LRU pointers, and frequency counts.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The caching architecture combines smart client routing, a distributed hashing ring, and node-level memory engines.
bullets: Smart Client Routing: Clients maintain a local view of the consistent hash ring, hashing keys directly to target nodes without intermediate proxy hops.
Consistent Hash Ring (ZooKeeper / Gossip): Discovers node health and maintains virtual node assignments across the hash circle.
Cache Worker Node: Runs multi-threaded network event loops (epoll/kqueue) reading from segregated in-memory partitions.
L1 Near-Cache: A small in-process cache inside application pods that absorbs ultra-hot keys with short 1-second TTLs.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: A distributed cache must route keys efficiently and evict data without letting locks stall request threads.
bullets: Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes: Map nodes to multiple points (e.g., 256 vnodes per server) on a 2^32 integer ring. When a server fails, its keys are redistributed evenly across all remaining servers rather than overloading a single neighbor.

Segmented LRU and W-TinyLFU: Traditional LRU suffers from cache pollution when a sequential batch scan flushes out popular items. W-TinyLFU uses a Bloom filter-like Count-Min Sketch to admit new keys only if their frequency exceeds the eviction candidate.
Lock-free eviction: Partition the cache into independent segments (like Java's `ConcurrentHashMap`), each with its own eviction list, eliminating cross-core lock contention.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Production caching failures frequently cascade into database outages. Defensive mechanisms are required to keep the storage tier safe.
bullets: Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): When a hot key expires, thousands of concurrent requests miss and query the database simultaneously. Solve this using Singleflight request coalescing (only one thread fetches from the database while others await the result) and probabilistic early recomputation (XFetch).

Cache Penetration: Requests for non-existent keys bypass the cache and hit the database directly. Use a Bloom filter at the cache layer to reject invalid keys, or cache null values with a short 30-second TTL.
Hot Key Mitigation: Replicate ultra-popular keys across multiple nodes by appending random suffixes (`item_123#1`, `item_123#2`) or serving them from in-process L1 memory.

tradeOffs.option: Smart Client Routing (Direct to Cache Node)
tradeOffs.pros: Zero proxy hop latency; sub-millisecond response times; no central load balancer bottleneck.
tradeOffs.cons: Clients must maintain cluster topology state; updating the hash ring requires notifying all clients.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput internal microservices with low latency budgets (Memcached, Redis Cluster clients).

tradeOffs.pros: Clients remain simple and stateless; centralized connection pooling and security enforcement.
tradeOffs.cons: Adds 0.5 to 1ms of extra network hop latency; proxy tier requires separate scaling and maintenance.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Polyglot environments where maintaining smart client libraries in multiple languages is impractical.

tradeOffs.pros: W-TinyLFU delivers 10 to 20% higher hit ratios by resisting cache pollution from one-off sequential scans.
tradeOffs.cons: Slightly higher CPU overhead for frequency tracking compared to a basic doubly-linked LRU list.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Modern production caches with mixed read/scan workloads (Caffeine, Redis 6+ LFU).

interviewTip: When asked how to prevent cache stampedes, explain Singleflight coalescing: only one request goes to the database while others wait on a shared channel. Combine this with consistent hashing virtual nodes to explain how the cluster survives node additions and failures.
